name: Self-Driving Laboratories
title: Self-Driving Laboratories
answer: Self-driving laboratories are research systems that combine robotic automation, laboratory instruments, and artificial intelligence to run experiments with limited human intervention. They are used in chemistry, materials science, biology, and drug discovery, where many experiments can be planned and executed in a loop. The scope includes the software that selects experiments, the hardware that performs them, and the data systems that record results. These labs do not replace scientists entirely, because humans still set goals, constraints, and safety rules. The field sits within laboratory automation and simulation, and it draws on machine learning, robotics, and control theory.

sections.body: Self-driving laboratories are research systems that combine robotic automation, laboratory instruments, and artificial intelligence to run experiments with limited human intervention. They are used in chemistry, materials science, biology, and drug discovery, where many experiments can be planned and executed in a loop. The scope includes the software that selects experiments, the hardware that performs them, and the data systems that record results. These labs do not replace scientists entirely, because humans still set goals, constraints, and safety rules. The field sits within laboratory automation and simulation, and it draws on machine learning, robotics, and control theory.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A self-driving lab runs on a mix of physical and computational infrastructure. On the physical side, it uses robotic arms, liquid handlers, automated synthesis platforms, and analytical instruments such as spectrometers and chromatographs. On the computational side, it relies on orchestration software to schedule tasks, data pipelines to move results, and machine learning models to propose the next experiment. Simulation environments and digital twins can run virtual experiments before they are attempted on real equipment. Compute may be local or in the cloud, and interoperability standards help different instruments and software components work together.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done in a closed loop. A human or an algorithm defines an objective, such as finding a material with a target property or a reaction with high yield. The system then generates candidate experiments, often using Bayesian optimization or active learning, and sends them to the robotic platform. After each experiment, analytical instruments measure the outcome, and the data is fed back to update the model. The loop repeats until a stopping condition is met, and every step is logged for reproducibility.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance are central concerns for self-driving laboratories. Provenance means tracking the origin of samples, the version of the software, and the parameters of each experiment, so that results can be audited and reproduced. Risks include chemical or biological hazards if the system runs unattended, and the possibility that a model proposes unsafe or wasteful experiments. Intellectual property questions arise about who owns discoveries made with minimal human input, and liability questions arise if an automated system causes damage. Many groups address these issues with human oversight, access controls, and detailed audit trails.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward tighter integration between AI planning and robotic execution. Future systems may use large language models to help design experiments or interpret literature, and cloud labs may allow remote users to run experiments without owning the hardware. Standardization of data formats and instrument interfaces is likely to make it easier to assemble labs from different vendors. There is also growing interest in self-driving labs for biology and materials discovery, where the search space is vast. The main challenges ahead are reproducibility, safety, and ensuring that the benefits are widely accessible.
